newsitem.title: USA: Hilton bonds have coupon reset to ease fears.
newsitem.headline: Hilton bonds have coupon reset to ease fears.

text.p: A coupon reset feature embedded in Hilton Hotels Corp's upcoming $300 million 10-year debt offering eases the credit risk from its outstanding hostile bid for ITT Corp but will probably go unused, analysts and market sources said.
The provision ensures a mimimum bump up of 175 basis points in yield should the assumption and/or use of debt prompt a downgrade to junk bond status within three years.
But such a downgrade seems extremely unlikely, analysts said, given Hilton's deep commitment to its prized investment grade ratings.

"If they do the ITT transaction, it's our understanding that we would sit down with them and discuss the parameters needed to achieve an investment grade rating...and they would structure it in a way to achieve that," said S&P corporate ratings analyst Greg Zappin.
"It's our understanding that it is (Hilton's) intention to remain investment grade," he added.

Hilton's potential debt load increase prompted both S&P and Moody's Investors Service in January to review their ratings for possible downgrade. As it stands, Hilton's offer for ITT is valued at $10.5 billion, including the assumption of approximately $4 billion ITT debt.
A single- or double-notch downgrade may still not trip the reset feature -- current BBB-plus/Baa1 ratings from the two agencies stand three full notches above junk status.

Moody's analyst Frances Schulman underscored the provision was used primarily to secure a better coupon amid takover uncertainty. Asked about a triple-notch downgrade, however, she said "If you issue enough debt, anything is possible."
Bonds could be repriced in an orderly fashion in event of a rating cut within the investment grade ranks, a source said.

Wall Street analysts said the provision will serve to remove any degree of doubt investors might have about the credit as hostile takeover talk looms. That protection should ultimately lead to a tighter priced deal, they said.

"The (feature) just gives investors a little added protection without costing Hilton," said an analyst at a Wall Street investment firm. "Hilton said they had three goals and one of them is to maintain an investment grade rating...this (provision) actually gives them more of an incentive."

Although Hilton's dedication to an investment grade rating appears genuine, investors also realize that Chief Executive Officer Stephen Bollenbach "is not afraid of using leverage," another analyst said.
"It's there to make investors believe (Bollenbach) is walking his talk," the analyst said.
The coupon reset feature has not been popular since the heyday of leveraged buyouts of the mid- to late-1980s, dealers said, many of which contributed to a widespread erosion in credit quality.

For the Hilton deal, it will add 175 basis points in yield if ratings fall to Ba1/BB-plus; 210 basis points if they fall to Ba2/BB; 250 basis points to Ba3/BB-minus; and 325 basis points to B1/B-plus or below.
The deal is expected to price on Thursday via lead manager Merrill Lynch & Co Inc. Merrill Lynch declined comment.
